---
title: Linting
description: >
  This section provides instructions and examples for using the Panache linter,
  which checks for correctness issues and best practice violations in your
  Markdown documents.
---

Panache includes a built-in linter that checks for correctness issues and best
practice violations in your Markdown documents. It catches syntax errors,
heading hierarchy issues, broken references, and citation problems. It also
flags prose conventions that need the author's judgment.

::: {.callout-tip}
For the full catalog of built-in lint rules, the diagnostic codes each rule
emits, severity, and auto-fix support, see the [Lint Rules
reference](../reference/linter-rules.qmd).
:::

## Philosophy

The linter focuses on semantic correctness. The formatter handles routine style
consistency, which you can check with `panache format --check`.

Some prose edits depend on language or author intent. The linter flags these
edits and offers fixes you can review. For example, `space-before-punctuation`
flags spaces before punctuation without removing them during formatting. Its
fixes are unsafe because the spacing may be intentional.

## CLI Usage

### Basic Linting

To lint a single file and show diagnostics, run this:

```bash
panache lint document.qmd
```

To lint multiple files at once, you can specify them one-by-one:

```bash
panache lint file1.md file2.qmd file3.Rmd
```

If you want to lint all supported files in a directory, use:

```bash
panache lint .
panache lint docs/
```

`panache lint` supports glob patterns as well:

```bash
panache lint 'src/**/*.qmd'
```

### Lint from stdin

You can also pipe content through the linter:

```bash
cat document.qmd | panache lint # or `panache lint < document.qmd`
```

Or with a here-document:

```bash
panache lint <<'EOF'
# H1
### H3
EOF
```

### Apply Automatic Fixes

Panache can automatically fix certain types of issues:

```bash
panache lint --fix document.qmd
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Auto-fix modifies files in place. Always commit your changes first or use
version control.
:::

#### Safe and Unsafe Fixes

Fixes come in two safety levels. A plain `--fix` applies only **safe** fixes,
which tidy syntax without changing what the document means. Fixes that could
change meaning---such as the `empty-values` fix, which deletes the empty key---
are **unsafe** and skipped by default. When unsafe fixes are available but were
not applied, the CLI reports how many; pass `--unsafe-fixes` to apply them too:

```bash
panache lint --fix --unsafe-fixes document.qmd
```

`--unsafe-fixes` only takes effect alongside `--fix`. See [Fix
safety](../reference/linter-rules.qmd#fix-safety) for details, including how
unsafe fixes behave in the editor.

### CI Mode

`panache lint` exits with code 1 whenever any violations are found, so it works
in a CI/CD pipeline without any extra flags:

```bash
panache lint .
```

::: {.callout-note}
The `--check` flag is deprecated and now a no-op: exiting non-zero on violations
is the default behavior. It is still accepted for backward compatibility but
will be removed in a future release.
:::

### Message Format

Use `--message-format` to control diagnostic verbosity:

```bash
panache lint --message-format human document.qmd # default rich output
panache lint --message-format short document.qmd # GNU-style one-line diagnostics
```

Human output highlights the reported issue and shows any suggested fix on a
separate `help` line. The highlighted location matches short output, even when
the fix edits a larger range of source text.

## Lint Rules

Panache includes several built-in lint rules that analyze document structure and
content. See the [Lint Rules reference](../reference/linter-rules.qmd) for the
complete catalog, including each rule's diagnostic codes, severity, auto-fix
status, and configuration requirements.

The
[`html-unclosed-attribute`](../reference/linter-rules.qmd#html-unclosed-attribute)
rule warns about missing closing quotes in HTML attributes, including tags that
the Markdown parser treats as ordinary text. It runs when raw HTML is enabled
and highlights the opening quote. The author chooses where to close the value.

## External Linters

Panache can integrate with external code linters to check code blocks within
your documents.

### Configuration

Enable external linters in your configuration file:

```toml
[linters]
r = "arity"
julia = "fatou"
latex = "badness"
python = "ruff"
sh = "shellcheck"
js = "eslint"
go = "staticcheck"
rust = "clippy"
```

Available external linters:

  | Language              | Linter        | Description                         |
  | --------------------- | ------------- | ----------------------------------- |
  | R                     | `arity`       | R linter with JSON diagnostics      |
  | R                     | `jarl`        | R linter with JSON diagnostics      |
  | Julia                 | `fatou`       | Julia linter with JSON diagnostics  |
  | LaTeX                 | `badness`     | LaTeX linter with JSON diagnostics  |
  | Python                | `ruff`        | Python linter with JSON diagnostics |
  | Shell                 | `shellcheck`  | Shell linter with JSON diagnostics  |
  | JavaScript/TypeScript | `eslint`      | JS/TS linter with JSON diagnostics  |
  | Go                    | `staticcheck` | Go linter with JSON diagnostics     |
  | Rust                  | `clippy`      | Rust linter with JSON diagnostics   |

### How External Linters Work

External linters analyze code blocks and executable inline expressions:

1. **Collection**: Code blocks and executable inline expressions of the target
   language are extracted in document order, with any enclosing container syntax
   (block quote markers, list item indentation) stripped so the linter sees
   valid code
2. **Concatenation**: Code that shares an execution context is joined, retaining
   blank-line padding where possible
3. **Analysis**: The external linter analyzes the combined code, treating inline
   expression results as used values
4. **Mapping**: Diagnostics are mapped back to original document positions,
   accounting for each line's stripped container prefix

::: {.callout-note}
This approach correctly handles stateful code. If a variable is defined in one
executable code block and used in another executable block or an inline
expression, the linter sees both the definition and the use.
:::

Under the Quarto flavor, inline analysis supports `` `r expression` ``,
`` `{r} expression` ``, `` `{python} expression` ``, and
`` `{julia} expression` ``. R Markdown supports the classic R form. These follow
the `rmarkdown-inline-code` and `quarto-inline-code` extension settings.
Ordinary code spans and escaped examples using extra backticks or doubled braces
are excluded.

Under the Quarto flavor, executable chunks and inline expressions share a lint
context for each language. Displayed fences such as ```` ```r ```` and
```` ```{.r} ````, and chunks with a literal `eval: false` (or `eval=FALSE`),
are each linted independently. Their assignments cannot satisfy references in
executable code or conflict with its definitions. They still receive diagnostics
and fixes. Hashpipe options override options in the fence header.
Expression-valued options such as `eval: !expr false` leave the chunk in the
executable context. Options such as `echo: false` and `include: false` hide
output but leave the chunk in the executable context. Panache uses explicit cell
options for this grouping; it does not evaluate option expressions or infer
runtime changes to defaults.

Under the Quarto flavor, external linters also analyze code from `include`
shortcodes in inclusion order. Nested include paths resolve relative to the main
document; paths starting with `/` resolve from the project root. Repeated
includes contribute code at each occurrence. An include that is missing,
unreadable, or cyclic prevents external analysis of that execution context and
produces an include diagnostic instead.

Panache uses known parent documents when linting a partial directly. It
discovers parents among the project's render targets and the documents selected
for the current lint command. Without a known parent, the partial is analyzed on
its own. Diagnostics point to the file containing the code. A finding specific
to a parent names that parent in a note; identical findings from several parents
are combined.

`lint --fix` edits only the command's target files, including files selected by
a directory scan. Findings in other included files are reported but do not
modify those files. A fix in shared source is available only when every known
execution context and repeated occurrence agrees on its edits, even with
`--unsafe-fixes`. Fixes spanning source files are omitted. With
`--stdin-filename`, include resolution uses that filename and the supplied input
replaces its on-disk contents for analysis; fixes still write only to stdout.
For every flavor, the stdin filename also supplies the document directory for
external linter configuration and relative command and argument paths. ESLint
and Clippy use isolated temporary directories instead. Without a stdin filename,
relative linter commands resolve from Panache's working directory, including
commands for ESLint and Clippy.

Panache bypasses the lint cache when a contributing external linter may read
configuration outside Panache's tracked inputs, including Ruff's project
configuration and ESLint's command or argument overrides. This includes a
partial whose own Panache configuration does not enable the parent's linter.
Arity, Fatou, and Badness can reuse cached results with `--no-config` and the
preset executable. The unmodified ESLint preset also disables configuration
lookup.

::: {.callout-note}
For a code block nested in a block quote or list item, an autofix that would add
or remove whole lines cannot be applied without disturbing the surrounding
container syntax, so such fixes are dropped and only the diagnostic is reported.
Fixes that stay within a single line apply normally.
:::

Inline fixes must stay within expression content. Fixes that cross expression
boundaries, introduce backticks or line breaks, remove existing line breaks, or
leave an empty expression are omitted while retaining the diagnostic.

### Example

Document with multiple R code blocks:

````markdown
---
title: "Analysis"
---

```{{r}}
x <- 10
```

Some text between blocks.

```{{r}}
y <- x + 5
```
````

With `[linters] r = "jarl"` configured, `jarl` analyzes both blocks together and
correctly understands that `x` is defined before it's used. Similarly, with
`[linters] python = "ruff"`, Ruff can lint Python code blocks and map
diagnostics back to the original document.

### Behavior

Language matching
:   Case-insensitive matching of code block language to linter configuration

Error handling
:   Missing linter executables log a warning and skip gracefully

Compatibility checks
:   External linters only run for their supported languages. Unsupported
    mappings in `[linters]` (for example, `bash = "jarl"`) are skipped with a
    warning.

Timeout
:   30-second timeout per linter invocation

Line accuracy
:   Diagnostics report exact line and column positions in the original document
    after mapping the linter's ranges through code chunk and container prefixes.
    For Jarl, Panache uses byte ranges, which remain accurate when Jarl 0.5
    reports an inconsistent column after an initial blank line.

Auto-fixes
:   Supported for external linters that return fix edits with mappable ranges
    (currently `arity`, `fatou`, `badness`, `jarl`, `ruff`, and `eslint`). Fixes
    that the linter marks as unsafe (`arity`, `fatou`, `badness`, `jarl`,
    `ruff`) are only applied under `--unsafe-fixes`. Requires badness 0.14+ for
    LaTeX (earlier versions lack JSON output and are skipped). Jarl's legacy
    `content`/`start`/`end` fixes (0.5), `content`/`range` fixes (0.6), and
    `edits`/`safety` fixes (0.7) are recognized by JSON shape, without inferring
    a version. Legacy single-edit shapes (0.5 and 0.6 output) require
    `--unsafe-fixes`; those releases do not serialize safety with the fix. The
    modern edits shape preserves Jarl's explicit safety. Additional metadata is
    accepted, but conflicting shapes are rejected. Multi-edit fixes are mapped
    atomically: if any edit cannot be mapped or edits overlap, no part of the
    fix is offered. Unrecognized shapes, mapping failures and overlaps retain
    the diagnostic and add a visible explanatory note. Decoder errors and fix
    JSON in notes are limited to 256 characters each (with an ellipsis when
    truncated) to keep CLI and LSP diagnostics readable.

### Where External Linters Run

CLI
:   Diagnostics appear in `panache lint` output

LSP
:   Diagnostics appear inline in your editor with live updates

## Ignore Directives

You can selectively disable linting for specific regions using HTML comment
directives:

### Ignore Linting Only

Use `panache-ignore-lint-start` and `panache-ignore-lint-end` to suppress lint
warnings:

```markdown
Normal content will be linted.

<!-- panache-ignore-lint-start -->
#### This heading skip won't trigger heading-hierarchy warning
<!-- panache-ignore-lint-end -->

Back to normal linting.
```

This is useful for:

- Intentional heading level skips for specific formatting
- Generated content with unusual structure
- Third-party content you don't control
- Documentation examples showing bad practices

#### Ignore Both Formatting and Linting

Use `panache-ignore-start` and `panache-ignore-end` to disable both:

```markdown
<!-- panache-ignore-start -->
#### Unusual   structure   here
Both formatting and linting ignored in this region
<!-- panache-ignore-end -->
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Note on Directive Behavior**: Lint rules still "see" content in ignored
regions when tracking context (e.g., for heading hierarchy), but diagnostics
from ignored regions are filtered out. This ensures rules maintain proper state
across the document.
:::

See [Formatting](formatting.qmd) for more information about formatting-specific
ignore directives.

## Configuration

Use `[lint]` to choose which built-in rules run. Rules use the exact names in
the [rule reference](../reference/linter-rules.qmd).

By default, Panache runs every rule marked **Default: On**. Use `ignore` to
disable rules and `extend-select` to enable opt-in rules alongside the defaults:

```toml
[lint]
ignore = ["heading-hierarchy"]
extend-select = ["quarto-schema-unknown-key"]
```

To run only specific rules, use `select`, which replaces the defaults:

```toml
[lint]
select = ["undefined-references", "duplicate-reference-labels"]
```

Panache starts with the defaults or `select`, adds `extend-select`, then removes
`ignore`. An empty `select = []` disables the defaults; `extend-select` can
still add rules. Selecting a rule does not override its flavor or extension
requirements. Parser errors and external linters are configured separately.

For a single CLI run, use comma-separated rule names with `--select`,
`--extend-select`, or `--ignore`:

```sh
panache lint --select undefined-references,duplicate-reference-labels document.qmd
panache lint --extend-select quarto-schema-unknown-key document.qmd
panache lint --ignore heading-hierarchy document.qmd
```

`--select` and `--ignore` replace their corresponding configuration lists.
`--extend-select` adds to the configured additions. Pass `--select ""` to
disable the defaults or `--ignore ""` to clear configured ignores.

### Spacing Before Punctuation

The `space-before-punctuation` rule checks spaces before `.`, `,`, and `;` in
prose by default. To allow this spacing, disable the rule:

```toml
[lint]
ignore = ["space-before-punctuation"]
```

Review these warnings, then apply their fixes with
`panache lint --fix --unsafe-fixes document.qmd`. A plain `--fix` leaves this
spacing unchanged. French documents retain spaces before semicolons when
identified by YAML `lang:` or the `[format].lang` fallback.

## LSP Integration

When using the Panache language server, lint diagnostics appear live in your
editor as you type:

- Squiggly underlines for errors and warnings
- Hover tooltips showing diagnostic messages
- Code actions for auto-fixes (e.g., fix heading hierarchy)

See [Editor Setup](lsp.qmd) to connect your editor and [Language
Server](language-server.qmd#live-diagnostics) for diagnostic behavior and [code
actions](language-server.qmd#code-actions).

## Examples

### Example 1: Heading Hierarchy

Before:

```markdown
# Main Title

### Skipped Level

#### Another Skip
```

Run linter:

```bash
panache lint document.qmd
```

Output:

```
warning: [heading-hierarchy] Heading level skipped from h1 to h3; expected h2
 --> document.qmd:3:1
  |
3 | ### Skipped Level
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

warning: [heading-hierarchy] Heading level skipped from h3 to h4; expected h3
 --> document.qmd:5:1
  |
5 | #### Another Skip
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

Apply auto-fix:

```bash
panache lint --fix document.qmd
```

After:

```markdown
# Main Title

## Skipped Level

### Another Skip
```

### Example 2: Duplicate References

Before:

```markdown
See [example1] and [example2].

[example1]: https://first.com
[example1]: https://second.com
[example2]: https://other.com
```

Run linter:

```bash
panache lint document.qmd
```

Output:

```
warning[duplicate-reference-labels]: Duplicate reference definition 'example1'
  --> document.qmd:4:1
note: First defined here:
  --> document.qmd:3:1
```

Resolution (manual):

```markdown
See [example1] and [example2].

[example1]: https://first.com
[example2]: https://other.com
```

### Example 3: Citation Validation

Before (with `refs.bib` configured):

```markdown
---
bibliography: refs.bib
---

See @existingkey and @missingkey.
```

Run linter:

```bash
panache lint document.qmd
```

Output:

```
warning[citation-keys]: Citation key 'missingkey' not found in bibliography
  --> document.qmd:5:24
```

Resolution: Add the citation to `refs.bib` or remove the reference.
